lessons.title: Brackets, factors and formulae
lessons.programRef: Cameroon secondary (general education) Mathematics programme, Form 2 (MINESEC) — to be checked against the official programme
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Expand a product of two brackets
Factorise by taking out a common factor
Change the subject of a simple formula
reviewNotes: Trinomial factorisation (x² + bx + c) and difference of two squares are left for Form 3.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Expanding two brackets
blocks.md: Multiply **each term of the first bracket by each term of the second**, then collect like terms: $(x + 2)(x + 3) = x^2 + 3x + 2x + 6 = x^2 + 5x + 6$. For a minus sign: $(2x - 1)(x + 4) = 2x^2 + 8x - x - 4 = 2x^2 + 7x - 4$. An area picture shows all four products.

blocks.title: Factorising: common factor
blocks.md: **Factorising** is the opposite of expanding. Find the largest number and the lowest power of a letter that divide every term and write it outside a bracket: $6x^2 + 9x = 3x(2x + 3)$. Check by expanding the answer.

blocks.title: Changing the subject
blocks.md: To make a letter the subject, undo the operations around it, doing the same to both sides. From $P = 2(l + w)$: divide by 2 to get $\frac{P}{2} = l + w$, then subtract w: $l = \frac{P}{2} - w$. From $v = u + at$: $t = \frac{v - u}{a}$.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Writing $(x + 3)^2 = x^2 + 9$: it is $(x + 3)(x + 3) = x^2 + 6x + 9$.
- Taking out a factor but leaving a term without a factor in the bracket: $6x^2 + 9x = 3x(2x + 3)$, not $3x(2x + 9)$.
- Moving a term across the equals sign without changing its sign.

blocks.title: Example 1: expand
blocks.statement: A garden has length (x + 5) m and width (x + 2) m. Expand its area and find it when x = 3.

blocks.title: Example 2: factorise and change the subject
blocks.statement: Factorise 6x² + 9x. Make l the subject of P = 2(l + w).
steps: The common factor of 6x² and 9x is 3x. 6x² ÷ 3x = 2x and 9x ÷ 3x = 3, so 3x(2x + 3).
Divide P = 2(l + w) by 2: P/2 = l + w.

lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Solve linear inequalities, including multiplying by a negative number
Show the solution on a number line
reviewNotes: Compound and simultaneous inequalities are left for Form 3.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Equations with fractions
blocks.md: Multiply **every term** by the denominator to clear the fraction. $\frac{x}{3} + 2 = 7$: subtract 2 to get $\frac{x}{3} = 5$, then multiply by 3: x = 15. $\frac{2x - 1}{3} = 5$: multiply by 3: 2x − 1 = 15, so x = 8. Always check by substituting.

blocks.title: Inequalities
blocks.md: The symbols are: < (less than), > (greater than), ≤ (less than or equal to), ≥ (greater than or equal to). An inequality has **many solutions**: x > 4 is true for 5, 6, 4.5, 100 and so on. On a number line an **open circle** shows that the end point is not included; a **closed circle** shows that it is included.

blocks.caption: Number line showing x > 4: open circle at 4, arrow to the right.
blocks.alt: A number line from 0 to 8 with an open circle at 4 and a shaded line to the right.

blocks.title: Solving inequalities
blocks.md: Solve like an equation (same operation on both sides), with one big difference: **when you multiply or divide by a negative number, reverse the inequality sign.** −2x ≤ 6 gives x ≥ −3.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Forgetting to reverse the sign when dividing by a negative number.
- Using a closed circle for > or <.
- Multiplying only one term by the denominator in an equation with fractions.

blocks.title: Example 1: fractions
steps: (b) Multiply by 3: 2x − 1 = 15, so 2x = 16 and x = 8. Check (16 − 1)/3 = 5.

blocks.title: Example 2: inequalities
blocks.statement: Solve 3x − 2 > 10 and show it on a number line. Then solve −2x ≤ 6.
steps: 3x > 12, so x > 4. Open circle at 4 and an arrow to the right.
Divide −2x ≤ 6 by −2 and reverse the sign: x ≥ −3.

lessons.title: Coordinates and straight-line graphs
lessons.programRef: Cameroon secondary (general education) Mathematics programme, Form 2 (MINESEC) — to be checked against the official programme
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Plot points in the four quadrants
Make a table of values and draw a straight line
Find the gradient and y-intercept of y = mx + c
Use a straight-line graph to solve a problem
reviewNotes: The fare formulas are invented for practice, not real taxi tariffs.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Coordinates
blocks.md: A point is given by an ordered pair (x, y): x tells how far along the horizontal axis, y how far up the vertical axis. The axes meet at the **origin** O(0, 0) and divide the plane into four **quadrants**. The point (−2, 3) is 2 left and 3 up.

blocks.title: Drawing a line
blocks.md: To draw y = 2x + 1 make a **table of values**: choose x = −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3 and calculate y = −3, −1, 1, 3, 5, 7. Plot the points; they lie on a straight line. Join them with a ruler and label the line. Two points are enough, a third checks.

blocks.title: Gradient and intercept
blocks.md: For y = mx + c the number m is the **gradient** (steepness): rise ÷ run. The number c is the **y-intercept**, where the line crosses the y-axis. y = 2x + 1 has gradient 2 and y-intercept 1; the line y = −x + 4 slopes down.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Plotting (x, y) as (y, x).
- Mixing negative numbers in the table: with y = 2x + 1 and x = −2, y = −3, not 5.
- Reading the gradient from the wrong scale when the axes have different scales.

blocks.title: Example 1: table and line
blocks.statement: Draw y = 2x + 1 for x from −2 to 3 and state the gradient.
steps: Plot and join them: a straight line through (0, 1).

blocks.title: Example 2: a taxi fare
blocks.statement: A taxi in Bamenda charges F = 300 + 150d FCFA for a trip of d km. Find the fare for 4 km, and the distance for a fare of 1 500 FCFA.
steps: d = 8 km. The gradient 150 is the cost per km and 300 is the starting charge.

lessons.title: Sets: complement, three sets and problems
lessons.programRef: Cameroon secondary (general education) Mathematics programme, Form 2 (MINESEC) — to be checked against the official programme
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Use the complement A′ and the universal set
Draw and read a Venn diagram with three sets
Use n(A ∪ B ∪ C) for three sets
reviewNotes: The subsets count (2ⁿ) in the last self-check is extension content; check against the official scheme.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Set notation
blocks.md: The **complement** A′ is the set of elements in ξ that are not in A. The set {x : x is an even number, x < 10} reads 'the set of x such that x is even and less than 10' and equals {2, 4, 6, 8}. The notation A ∩ B ∩ C means the elements in all three sets.

blocks.title: Venn diagrams with three sets
blocks.md: Draw three overlapping circles in a rectangle. There are **eight regions**. Work from the middle outwards: first A ∩ B ∩ C, then the regions with two sets only (subtract the centre), then the regions with one set only, and finally the outside. The total of all regions is n(ξ).

blocks.caption: Venn diagram of three sports: 10, 8, 6 only; 5, 4, 3 two sports; 2 all three; 22 none.
blocks.alt: Three overlapping circles with numbers in all regions and 22 outside.

blocks.title: Counting formula
blocks.md: For three sets, the number in at least one set is:
blocks.tex: n(A \cup B \cup C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) - n(A \cap B) - n(A \cap C) - n(B \cap C) + n(A \cap B \cap C)

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Writing n(A ∩ B) in the 'A and B only' region: that region excludes the centre.
- Forgetting the elements outside all three circles.
- Confusing A′ (complement) with the empty set.

blocks.title: Example 1: fill a diagram
blocks.statement: In a school of 60 students: n(A) = 21 play football, n(B) = 18 volleyball, n(C) = 15 athletics; n(A ∩ B) = 7, n(A ∩ C) = 6, n(B ∩ C) = 5 and n(A ∩ B ∩ C) = 2. Find how many play only football.
steps: Centre = 2. A and B only = 7 − 2 = 5; A and C only = 6 − 2 = 4; B and C only = 5 − 2 = 3.

blocks.title: Example 2: none of them
blocks.statement: Using Example 1, find how many students play none of the three sports.
blocks.answer: **22 students play none of the three.**
